# Scientific society or academy (`scientific_academy`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/institutions.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Institutions, law & governance (`institutions`)
- Deps: helped by scientific_method, reproducibility_open_publication, scientific_journal, postal_system
- Core idea: A chartered society of investigators that meets on fixed days to watch experiments performed, records them in minutes, corresponds with others abroad, and prints what it finds. Nothing is accepted on authority (the Royal Society's motto: nullius in verba); claims are shown before witnesses and can be repeated. A dated register of communications settles who was first, which removes the main reason for secrecy. To survive it needs a patron's charter, members' dues or a royal salary, a paid secretary and experimenter, and a firm rule to keep religion and politics out of its meetings.
- Pitfalls:
  - Depending on one patron: the Accademia del Cimento lasted ten years and died when its Medici sponsors lost interest (1667)
  - A talking club of gentlemen with no experiments, instruments or publication produces nothing
  - Shutting out craftsmen, instrument makers and physicians, who hold most of the practical knowledge
  - Allowing theological debate invites suppression (the first Lincei faded after Galileo's condemnation and its founder's death)
  - Picturing Baghdad's House of Wisdom as an academy of sciences: the sources show a palace library with translators and astronomers attached; its scale is debated
- History: greece: c. 387 BC – Plato's Academy; c. 335 BC Aristotle's Lyceum organises collective research; egypt: c. 280 BC – the Museum of Alexandria: salaried scholars, a library and common meals, funded by the Ptolemies; china: c. 318 BC – Jixia academy in Qi, where the state housed and paid scholars of rival schools; 8th c. Hanlin Academy, a body of court scholars; india: 14th–16th c. – the Kerala school of astronomy and mathematics, a teacher-pupil lineage without formal charter; islamic: c. 800–830 – the caliphal library (Bayt al-Hikma) at Baghdad with associated translators and astronomers under al-Ma'mun; 1259 Maragha and c. 1420 Samarkand observatories with staffs of scholars; europe: 1603 – Accademia dei Lincei, Rome; 1657 Accademia del Cimento, Florence; 1660 Royal Society (charter 1662); 1666 Académie royale des sciences, with salaried members; 1700 Berlin; 1724 St Petersburg; americas: 1743 – American Philosophical Society, Philadelphia
- Read:
  - Thomas Sprat, The History of the Royal Society of London (1667)
  - Michael Hunter, Establishing the New Science: The Experience of the Early Royal Society (1989)
  - Dimitri Gutas, Greek Thought, Arabic Culture (1998)
